transcript.text: Elena, let me address both questions directly. First, on omitting individual employee names: the DOJ Antitrust Division's Corporate Leniency Program requires the applicant to provide a full and frank disclosure of the conduct, which in practice includes identifying the individuals involved. The program's conditions obligate the company to cooperate fully, and that typically means naming the employees who participated in the coordinated bidding. Omitting individual names from the leniency application would create a significant tension with the program's disclosure requirements and could jeopardize our eligibility — particularly the requirement that we be first to report and provide complete information. So my legal assessment is that the leniency application cannot cleanly accommodate the protocol's requirement to omit individual employee names. That is a direct conflict we need to resolve with the audit committee. Second, on the 90-day independent pricing controls review: this requirement can run alongside the leniency application timeline without creating a sequencing problem. The leniency application itself focuses on disclosing the coordinated bidding conduct and seeking marker status. The independent pricing controls review is a separate compliance remediation measure that can proceed in parallel — it does not need to be completed before we file, and it does not need to be incorporated into the application itself. We can commit to the audit committee that the review will be completed within 90 days as a parallel track while the leniency application moves forward on its own timeline. So my bottom-line assessment: the 90-day pricing controls review is compatible with the leniency strategy and can run alongside it. The individual employee name omission is not compatible with the leniency program's disclosure requirements and creates a conflict that I recommend we take back to the audit committee to seek an adjustment — either a carve-out from the naming prohibition for purposes of the DOJ submission, or a protocol amendment that permits naming individuals in the leniency application while still omitting them from any other external disclosures. Elena, I would not recommend proceeding with a leniency application that omits employee names, as it risks our eligibility for the program.
